subject: Follow-up: token capacity playbook & streaming constraints (ShipMint pilot)
messages:
From: Rachel Kim <rachel.kim@redwood.com>
To: Elena Morris <elena@shipmint.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>
Date: Sun, 18 Apr 2027 15:04:00 -0700
Subject: Post-call recap + sizing asks (ShipMint pilot)

Hi Elena / Alex — thanks for the time today. Quick recap from our call and the items we need to move the pilot sizing forward. I captured the numbers as we discussed; please flag anything off.

TL;DR: baseline steady-state, peak crest, streaming vs non-streaming split, and sample payload sizes — these will drive the tokens/sec and concurrency math for pilot capacity.

What we heard today (please confirm):
- Steady-state interactive QPS: ~15 req/s during business hours (cart validation, recommendations)
- Average tokens per request (non-streaming): ~450 tokens (mostly short prompts + product context)
- Peak crest (flash sales / checkout) QPS: ~110 req/s (approx ~7x steady)
- Streaming sessions (voice assistant and checkout progress): ~55 concurrent streaming sessions at peak; streaming adds per-session token-rate of ~12 tokens/sec on average
- SLA targets: 95th pct latency target for interactive (non-streaming) = 350 ms; for streaming we discussed aiming for 95th < 700 ms
- Typical session length: 45–90s for streaming interactions; timeouts around 120s acceptable

Open clarifying asks (we need answers to finalize the capacity workbook):
1) Can you confirm the 450 tokens/request average and whether you include response tokens in that number?
2) Streaming vs non-streaming traffic split: is 60% streaming at peak accurate?
3) Any extended large-payload events (e.g., long transcripts or batched multi-turn uploads) we should model as outliers?
4) Are you willing to accept a fallback model (smaller quantized variant) for 5–10% of requests during extreme crest events in exchange for cost predictability?

Next steps:
- We’ll draft an initial pilot sizing recommendation and GPU pool suggestion (Marissa will lead the math) and share the workbook (pilot-sizing-workbook.xlsx).
- Can we schedule a 30-min follow-up on Tue or Wed to finalize values and sign off on the pilot SLOs? Here’s a placeholder meet: https://meet.google.com/rdw-shipmint-call

Attachments: ShipMint_SLOs_v2.pdf (you mentioned this exists) — if you can attach the latest version it will help.

Thanks,
Rachel

Subject: Re: Post-call recap + sizing asks (ShipMint pilot)

Thanks Rachel — this aligns closely with what we expected. Quick confirmations and a couple of clarifications below.

Confirmations:
- Average tokens/request: 450 tokens including both prompt and model response (we have short responses on average).
- Peak crest: 110–120 QPS is realistic for the first 6–8 weeks of marketing-led traffic spikes.
- Streaming concurrency: 50–60 concurrent sessions at peak; voice transcripts add ~10–15 tokens/sec once the user starts speaking.
- Session length: up to ~90s typical; we have a handful of long customer support flows that can hit ~180s but those are <1% of sessions.

SLO nuance: We care about perceived latency for streaming (time-to-first-token) — 95th < 500 ms would be ideal. For non-streaming interactive endpoints 95th < 350 ms is still our target.

Outliers and special events:
- We do have planned campaigns that might briefly drive 200–300 QPS for ~10 minutes (we’ll try to give heads-up via the shared Slack channel).
- We can tolerate a fallback to a smaller model for up to 10% of non-critical requests during extreme events if that’s the tradeoff for keeping latency within SLOs.

I attached the ShipMint_SLOs_v2.pdf with the internal SLO table and sample traces.

Thanks — Elena

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
To: Rachel Kim <rachel.kim@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 19 Apr 2027 11:05:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Post-call recap + sizing asks (ShipMint pilot)

Adding the sizing brain dump here so we can lock an initial pilot config. I ran the numbers based on Elena's confirmations.

Assumptions used:
- Steady: 15 QPS * 450 tokens = 6,750 tokens/sec sustained
- Peak crest: 120 QPS * 450 tokens = 54,000 tokens/sec crest
- Streaming (peak): 60 sessions * 12 tokens/sec = 720 tokens/sec (streaming aggregate) — note streaming is lower tokens/sec than non-streaming token bursts but increases concurrency and KV cache usage
- Transient campaign burst: 250 QPS * 450 tokens = 112,500 tokens/sec for ~10 minutes (we model as 10-minute crest)

Preliminary pilot recommendation (to start fast & cost-conscious):
- Start with a dedicated pool sized for sustained steady-state plus a safety buffer: aim for capacity to handle 2x steady sustained (≈13,500 tokens/sec) with autoscale headroom to cover 4–5x for medium bursts.
- Keep a small warm-bucket of burst capacity (on-demand nodes) to absorb the 10-minute campaign spikes — we recommend configuring burst policy that can spin additional nodes within ~90s.
- Model fallback: enable automatic fallback to a quantized 70B-variant for non-critical requests when crest > 6x steady; cap fallback to 10% of requests to match ShipMint tolerance.
- Streaming tuning: tune KV cache and reduce prefix recomputation for sessionized streams; we’ll propose lower-latency kernels and smaller transmit chunk sizes (we have a template config we’ll share).

Action items I’ll own:
1) Populate pilot-sizing-workbook.xlsx with the above scenarios and per-model GPU-hour estimates (shared in Drive).
2) Propose a 30-day pilot plan: baseline nodes, burst config, and rollback/fallback plan.
3) Draft the acceptance criteria: token/sec thresholds, time-to-first-token targets for streaming, and percent of requests allowed to fallback.

Can you confirm if ShipMint wants us to model the campaign burst as a single 10-minute crest (as Elena described) or a distributed burst (multiple 2–3 minute micro-crests)? That changes how aggressive we are on burst pool sizing.
